subject: Civil Engineering
title: Pounding Between Buildings
description: A 60-second lesson on Pounding Between Buildings.

hook.text: Two buildings stand inches apart. In an earthquake, they sway at different rates and collide.

buildup.text: Each building has its own natural period. Shorter ones sway fast, tall ones sway slow.

discovery.text: When they hit, columns at the contact point take enormous impact — causing local collapse.

twist.text: Floor slabs of adjacent buildings rarely align — a floor hits the other building's column.

climax.text: Seismic gaps — separation joints — keep buildings apart during maximum expected shaking.

punchline.text: Buildings need personal space. In earthquakes, neighbors too close become enemies.

quiz.question: Why is floor misalignment dangerous during building pounding?
options: It causes the floors to collapse on top of each other
One building's floor slab strikes the other's column, causing concentrated damage
The gap between floors lets earthquake waves enter the interior

details.summary: Seismic pounding occurs when adjacent buildings with different dynamic properties sway out of phase during an earthquake and collide at shared boundaries.
details.whyItMatters: Pounding has caused significant damage and collapse in urban earthquakes where buildings are constructed wall-to-wall with insufficient separation gaps.
takeaways: Adjacent buildings with different periods sway out of phase and can collide
Misaligned floor levels cause columns to be struck mid-height, concentrating damage
Building codes now require minimum separation gaps based on expected drift

faq.question: Why are misaligned floor levels between adjacent buildings so dangerous during pounding?
faq.answer: When floor slabs of one building align with columns of the adjacent building, pounding impacts hit columns at mid-height where they are weakest in shear. This can cause column shear failure and progressive collapse.

faq.question: How is pounding damage prevented in new construction?
faq.answer: Building codes require a seismic gap between adjacent structures equal to the sum of their maximum expected displacements, typically 50 to 200 millimeters for mid-rise buildings. Alternatively, buildings can be structurally connected to move together.
